lessons.title: Control any element with the global attributes
lessons.summary: Master the attributes every HTML element accepts — id, class, lang, dir, hidden, tabindex, contenteditable and the rest — and know exactly when each one is the right tool.
lessons.goal: Apply the full global attribute set correctly on a real page, including language, direction, visibility and focus control.
lessons.whyItMatters: Global attributes are the shared control panel of HTML: they work on every element and they quietly drive styling hooks, translation, screen-reader pronunciation, keyboard behavior and text direction. Senior developers are expected to know not just that these attributes exist but where each one breaks — title tooltips that touch users never see, positive tabindex values that wreck keyboard order, accesskey shortcuts that collide with assistive technology. Getting them right costs nothing; getting them wrong produces bugs that only appear for users you did not test with.

sections.heading: The identity attributes: id, class, style, title
sections.body:
Global attributes are the ones every HTML element accepts, from div to video. Four of them handle identity and presentation. id gives an element a name that must be unique in the document; it powers fragment links (page.html#pricing), label-to-input wiring (for="email"), aria-labelledby references and fast JavaScript lookup. Because so many systems key off it, a duplicated id is a real bug: getElementById and fragment navigation will silently pick the first match and ignore the rest.

class holds a space-separated list of reusable tokens, so class="card featured urgent" puts the element in three groups at once. Unlike id, classes are meant to repeat across elements — they are the primary hook for CSS and for selecting groups of elements in JavaScript. style injects CSS declarations directly onto one element. It works everywhere but scales terribly: inline styles cannot be reused, are painful to override, and mix presentation into markup, so in production they are mostly reserved for values computed at runtime, such as a progress bar width set by script.

title attaches advisory text that desktop browsers reveal as a small tooltip after the pointer rests on the element. The trap is the word 'desktop pointer': touch screens have no hover, keyboard navigation does not trigger it, and screen-reader support is inconsistent. The one place title has a solid, conventional role is expanding an abbreviation: <abbr title="User Experience">UX</abbr>. Anywhere else, if the information matters, it must also exist as visible text or a proper accessible name.

sections.heading: lang: tell machines what language they are reading
sections.body:
Every document should declare its main language on the root element: <html lang="en">. Screen readers use it to load the right pronunciation engine, browsers use it for hyphenation and quotation marks, translation tools use it to decide the source language, and spellcheckers use it to pick a dictionary. A page without lang forces every one of those systems to guess.

Because lang is global, you can override it on any element that switches language mid-page. A French quotation inside an English article gets lang="fr" on the blockquote; a Japanese product name gets lang="ja" on its span. A screen reader hitting that boundary switches voices instead of mangling the French with English phonetics — the difference between comprehensible and unlistenable.

Values are BCP 47 language tags: a lowercase language code (en, fr, ar), optionally followed by a region subtag (en-GB, pt-BR) when the regional difference matters for spelling or vocabulary. Keep the tag as short as it can be while still being accurate.

sections.heading: dir: writing direction, and why auto exists
sections.body:
dir controls the direction text flows and takes three values. ltr is the default left-to-right used by Latin, Greek and Cyrillic scripts. rtl flips the element for right-to-left scripts such as Arabic and Hebrew — not just alignment, but the placement of punctuation, the order of mixed numbers and text, and the side lists put their markers on. Like lang, set it on the smallest element that needs it; a whole-document Arabic site sets dir="rtl" on html, while one Arabic line in an English page sets it on that paragraph only.

The third value, auto, makes the browser look at the first strongly directional character inside the element and choose ltr or rtl from that. This is the correct setting for content you cannot predict — user comments, chat messages, echoed search queries — because it makes each element self-adjust. Hard-coding ltr on a comment box guarantees that the first Hebrew comment renders with its punctuation scrambled.

Pair dir with lang rather than treating one as a substitute for the other: lang says what the language is, dir says how the text flows, and right-to-left content needs both to be handled correctly.

sections.heading: hidden: the honest way to hide
sections.body:
hidden is a boolean attribute — its presence is the value, so <div hidden> is hidden and <div> is not. A hidden element is not rendered at all and is removed from the accessibility tree, meaning screen readers skip it exactly like sighted users do. This is what makes it more honest than most CSS hiding tricks: opacity: 0 and off-screen positioning leave content visible to assistive technology and to in-page search, creating ghost content only some users encounter.

Under the hood, browsers implement hidden as display: none in the user-agent stylesheet. That has one practical consequence: a CSS rule that sets display on the same element (a utility class with display: flex, for example) will override and defeat the attribute. If your codebase uses such utilities, a defensive rule like [hidden] { display: none !important; } keeps the attribute trustworthy.

Use hidden for content that is genuinely not part of the page right now — an inactive tab panel, a template area script will reveal, a dismissed banner. If content should be hidden visually but still announced to screen readers (like a text label for an icon button), that is the opposite requirement, and it is solved with a visually-hidden CSS class, not with hidden.

sections.heading: tabindex: three values, one trap
sections.body:
tabindex controls whether an element can receive keyboard focus and where it sits in the Tab order. Interactive elements — links, buttons, form fields — are focusable by default and need no tabindex at all. For everything else there are exactly two values worth using.

tabindex="0" inserts an element into the natural Tab order at the position its source markup dictates. It is how a custom widget built from a div (when a native element truly cannot be used) becomes reachable by keyboard. tabindex="-1" does the reverse trade: the element stays out of the Tab order but becomes focusable by script, so element.focus() works on it. That is the backbone of skip-link targets, error summaries and moving focus into freshly opened panels.

Positive values (tabindex="1" and up) are the trap. They create a priority lane: the browser visits all positive tabindex elements in ascending numeric order before any normally focusable element, regardless of where they appear on the page. Focus jumps around the layout, every later markup change forces renumbering, and users relying on the keyboard get an order that contradicts what they see. The professional rule is blunt: if the Tab order is wrong, fix the source order — never patch it with positive numbers.

sections.heading: contenteditable and spellcheck
sections.body:
contenteditable="true" turns any element into a live editing surface: the user can click in and type, and the DOM updates as they do. It is the foundation of rich-text editors, inline CMS editing and note apps, because unlike a textarea it can contain real markup — bold text, links, lists. Set contenteditable="false" on a child to lock a region inside an editable parent, such as a mention chip the user can delete but not edit character by character. The attribute is powerful and messy: browsers generate slightly different markup for the same edits, so production editors always normalize the output.

spellcheck="true" or "false" tells the browser whether to run its squiggly-underline checking on an element's editable text. It matters on form fields and contenteditable regions. Browsers check most text inputs by default, so the common real-world move is the opt-out: spellcheck="false" on fields holding usernames, code, IDs or API keys, where red squiggles are pure noise. The checker uses the dictionary implied by the element's lang, which is one more reason to declare language honestly.

sections.heading: draggable, translate and accesskey
sections.body:
draggable="true" opts an element into the native HTML drag-and-drop system; on most elements dragging does nothing until you set it, while links and images are draggable out of the box. The attribute only makes an element pick-up-able — the actual drop behavior requires the JavaScript drag events — and note that its values are the strings "true" and "false", so it is an enumerated attribute, not a boolean one like hidden. Native drag-and-drop is also mouse-only by design, so any interface built on it needs a keyboard alternative.

translate="no" marks content that machine translators should leave alone: brand names, code samples, personal names, legal boilerplate. Google Translate and similar services honor it, and it defaults to "yes" everywhere else. It is a small courtesy attribute that saves your product name from becoming a dictionary word in forty languages.

accesskey assigns a keyboard shortcut character to an element (accesskey="s" on a search field, for instance). In practice it is nearly always avoided: the modifier keys needed to trigger it differ by browser and operating system (Alt on Windows Chrome, Control+Option on macOS), users have no way to discover the shortcuts, and the chosen letters routinely collide with screen-reader and browser shortcuts, hijacking commands from the users who depend on them most. If an app needs shortcuts, implement them in JavaScript with a visible, documented shortcut list.

Two related niche attributes deserve a mention for touch devices: inputmode hints which virtual keyboard to show (inputmode="numeric" brings up digits) and enterkeyhint labels the Enter key itself (enterkeyhint="search" turns it into a Search action). Neither validates anything — they only shape the on-screen keyboard — but they noticeably polish mobile forms.

lessons.title: Store custom state on elements with data-* attributes
lessons.summary: Use data-* attributes to attach your own machine-readable data to markup, read it back through dataset, and style against it with CSS attribute selectors.
lessons.goal: Model product metadata and widget state with well-named data-* attributes that both CSS and JavaScript can consume.
lessons.whyItMatters: Every non-trivial front end needs to hang extra information on elements: which category a card belongs to, whether a panel is open, what configuration a widget should boot with. data-* attributes are the standards-blessed way to do that without inventing invalid attributes or abusing class names as data stores. They power filtering UIs, JS component configuration and CSS state styling in virtually every production codebase, so knowing their naming rules, the dataset camelCase mapping and their limits is table stakes for a working developer.

JavaScript reads the same values through element.dataset, where the hyphenated name data-stock-level becomes the camelCase property stockLevel. CSS can select on the attribute directly — [data-stock-level="low"] — which means state styling needs no extra classes. The three consumers (markup, script, style) all share one source of truth.

commonMistakes: Using uppercase or camelCase in the attribute itself (data-stockLevel). Attribute names are lowercased by the parser, so write data-stock-level in HTML and read dataset.stockLevel in JS.
Storing data that HTML already has semantics for — a publication date belongs in <time datetime="…">, a machine-readable value on an option belongs in value, not in data-*.
Forgetting that dataset values are always strings: dataset.price returns "89", so compare with Number(li.dataset.price) before doing math.
Treating data-* as private storage. Anything in the DOM is user-visible and user-editable via DevTools, so never put secrets or trust-sensitive values there.
lessons.proTip: In DevTools you can live-edit a data attribute and watch your [data-state] CSS respond instantly — a fast way to preview every visual state of a widget without triggering the JavaScript that drives it.

sections.heading: Why custom attributes need the data- prefix
sections.body:
HTML validates its attributes: writing category="packs" on an li is invalid markup, and worse, it gambles that no future HTML version will define a real category attribute with different behavior. The data-* family solves this by reserving an entire namespace for authors. Any attribute that starts with data- is guaranteed valid on any element, guaranteed meaningless to the browser's rendering and behavior, and guaranteed never to be claimed by a future specification.

That neutrality is the point. A data-* attribute does nothing on its own — no styling, no behavior, no semantics for assistive technology. It is inert storage that rides along with the element, waiting for your CSS or JavaScript to give it meaning. This makes it the correct home for information that belongs to your application rather than to the document: internal ids, states, configuration, sort keys.

The value is always a string. Numbers, booleans and even JSON can be stored, but they arrive back as text and your code owns the parsing. For one or two scalar values per element this is fine; if you find yourself stuffing large JSON blobs into attributes, the data usually belongs in a JavaScript module or a fetch response instead, with the element carrying only an id to look it up.

sections.heading: Naming rules that actually bite
sections.body:
The rules for the part after data- are strict enough to matter. Use lowercase letters, digits and hyphens: data-category, data-stock-level, data-sort-order-2. The name must not contain uppercase letters — the HTML parser lowercases attribute names anyway, so data-stockLevel silently becomes data-stocklevel and your camelCase intent is destroyed. It also must not start the custom part with a hyphen or contain characters like semicolons or spaces.

Multi-word names are written kebab-case with hyphens, exactly like CSS properties. This is not a style preference; it is the contract that makes the JavaScript mapping work, as the next section shows. Pick names that describe meaning rather than presentation: data-stock-level="low" survives a redesign, while data-color="orange" is a styling decision that has leaked into your data.

One more discipline point: keep names consistent across a codebase. If cards use data-category, do not let the search results page invent data-cat. Attribute names are an API between your markup, your scripts and your stylesheets — treat renames with the same care as renaming a function.

sections.heading: Reading and writing with dataset
sections.body:
Every element exposes its data-* attributes through the dataset property, a live map of the custom data. The naming bridge is mechanical: strip the data- prefix, then convert the remaining kebab-case to camelCase. data-category becomes dataset.category, data-stock-level becomes dataset.stockLevel, data-sort-order-2 becomes dataset.sortOrder-2's edge case aside — in practice, each hyphen-letter pair becomes an uppercase letter.

dataset is read-write. Assigning dataset.state = "open" creates or updates the data-state attribute in the DOM immediately, which means any CSS attribute selector watching that attribute restyles the element in the same frame. Deleting is delete el.dataset.state. Because these are real attributes, the values also show up in DevTools and in element.outerHTML, which makes debugging state trivial compared to state held only in JavaScript variables.

Two habits keep dataset code robust. First, remember everything is a string: dataset.price === 89 is always false; convert with Number() first. Second, for reading a single attribute you can also use getAttribute('data-price') — equivalent for reads, and sometimes clearer inside generic code that receives the attribute name as a string.

<button id="buy" data-sku="CS-1041" data-stock-level="low">Buy</button>
<script>
  const btn = document.getElementById('buy');
  btn.dataset.sku;               // "CS-1041"
  btn.dataset.stockLevel;        // "low"  (data-stock-level)
  btn.dataset.state = 'adding';  // writes data-state="adding"
  Number(btn.dataset.price);     // NaN-safe numeric read pattern
</script>

sections.heading: Styling against data with attribute selectors
sections.body:
CSS treats data-* like any other attribute, which unlocks state-driven styling without class churn. [data-state="open"] matches the exact value; [data-category] matches mere presence; and the operator variants cover partial matches — [data-sku^="CS-"] for prefix, [data-tags~="sale"] for a word in a space-separated list, [data-sku*="104"] for substring. Combined with element selectors, li[data-stock-level="low"] reads almost like a sentence.

The content property can even display attribute values directly: content: attr(data-category) inside an ::after rule prints the attribute's text into the page. This is genuinely useful for badges, counters and debug overlays, with two caveats — generated content is not selectable, and screen-reader support for it is uneven, so anything essential should be real text in the markup instead.

The payoff of this pattern is a clean division of labor: JavaScript flips one attribute (dataset.state = 'open'), and CSS owns everything visual about each state. No .is-open class-toggling scattered across the stylesheet, and the current state of any widget is readable at a glance in the Elements panel.

sections.heading: Three production patterns
sections.body:
State flags. A widget stores its current mode on its root element: data-state="closed", then "open", then perhaps "loading". Scripts switch the value, CSS styles each state, and tests can assert on it. Because the state lives in the DOM, server-side rendering can emit the correct initial state and the client picks it up seamlessly.

Widget configuration. A reusable script reads its options from the element it enhances: <div class="carousel" data-autoplay="true" data-interval="5000">. One script file serves every carousel on the site, each configured in markup by whoever writes the page — no per-instance JavaScript, and CMS editors can tune behavior without touching code.

Filtering and sorting lists. Each item carries its own facts — data-category, data-price — and the filter code simply hides items whose dataset does not match the active filters. The list can be re-rendered, paginated or reordered by the server and the filter logic never changes, because the data travels inside each element rather than in a parallel array that can drift out of sync.

sections.heading: When not to use data-*
sections.body:
The first question before reaching for data-* is whether HTML already has an attribute or element with the meaning you need. A machine-readable date belongs in <time datetime="2026-08-10">, not data-date. The value submitted by a form control belongs in value. A link's destination belongs in href. An image description belongs in alt. Custom attributes carry zero semantics, so every time you shadow a real feature with data-*, you lose the accessibility, SEO and browser behavior the native feature would have provided free.

The same logic covers state that assistive technology needs to know about. Whether a disclosure is expanded is not private app data — screen-reader users need it announced, so it belongs in aria-expanded, possibly mirrored by data-* for styling convenience but never replaced by it. Visibility belongs to hidden. Disabled state belongs to disabled. The rule of thumb: if a user or a machine outside your own scripts could benefit from the information, there is probably a standard home for it.

Finally, data-* is not storage for anything sensitive or large. It ships in the HTML payload, is visible to every user, and bloats the DOM if abused. Keep values short, public and element-scoped; put everything else behind your API.

lessons.title: Serve the right image to every screen with srcset, sizes and picture
lessons.summary: Solve the device-pixel-ratio and bandwidth problems with srcset x and w descriptors, use picture for art direction and format fallback, and stop layout shift with width, height and lazy loading.
lessons.goal: Upgrade a photo page so every image ships at the right resolution, in the best supported format, without shifting the layout.
lessons.whyItMatters: Images are the heaviest part of almost every page, and a single hard-coded src punishes someone: retina screens get blur, phones on mobile data get a desktop-sized download, and everyone gets layout jumps while images arrive. The responsive image toolkit — srcset, sizes, picture, loading and decoding — lets the browser pick the optimal file per device, which routinely cuts image bytes by half or more and directly improves Core Web Vitals. This is one of the highest-leverage performance skills a front-end developer owns.
steps: Read the device-pixel-ratio section to understand why one image file cannot fit all screens.
Fix the blurry logo with an x-descriptor srcset (task 1).
Give the hero image a w-descriptor srcset and a sizes attribute, and read how the browser chooses between candidates (tasks 2-3).
Add width, height, loading="lazy" and decoding="async" to the hero (task 4).
Wrap the sunset photo in a picture element offering AVIF and WebP before the JPEG fallback (tasks 5-6).
Press Run and confirm all six checks pass.
lessons.explanation: srcset lists the same photo at three real widths, each labeled with a w descriptor stating its pixel width. sizes tells the browser how wide the slot will render — full viewport width on small screens, 800 CSS pixels otherwise — so it can multiply slot width by device pixel ratio and download the smallest candidate that is still sharp. width and height give the browser the aspect ratio before any bytes arrive, reserving the exact space and preventing layout shift. loading="lazy" defers the download until the image nears the viewport, and decoding="async" keeps image decode work off the critical rendering path.
lessons.example:
A blog ships one 1600px hero JPEG to everyone. A phone on 4G downloads 380 KB to fill a 360px-wide slot, while the text below jumps down once the image finally arrives.

After the upgrade, the same phone downloads the 400w file at roughly 40 KB (or 800w if it has a 2x screen), the reserved aspect-ratio box means nothing moves when it loads, and browsers that support AVIF get an even smaller file through the picture element.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, add a 2x srcset to the logo, give the hero a w-descriptor srcset with a sizes attribute plus dimension and loading attributes, and wrap the sunset image in a picture element that offers AVIF and WebP sources before the JPEG fallback.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview looks unchanged — that is the point — but the markup now lets each browser pick the smallest sharp file, and all six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Writing srcset with w descriptors but omitting sizes. The browser then assumes the image is 100vw wide and often downloads a far larger file than the layout needs.
Confusing descriptors with units: it is 800w (image's real pixel width) and 2x (density), never 800px inside srcset.
Lazy-loading the hero image at the top of the page. Above-the-fold images should load eagerly — lazy-loading them delays Largest Contentful Paint instead of improving it.
Dropping width and height because CSS sets the size anyway. Without the intrinsic ratio the browser reserves zero height and the page reflows when the image decodes.
lessons.proTip: In Chrome DevTools, the img element's 'currentSrc' property (visible in the console via document.querySelector('img').currentSrc) shows exactly which srcset candidate the browser chose — resize the window and reload with DPR emulation to watch the choice change.

coding.intro: You will upgrade three images — a logo, a hero and a sunset photo — so each device downloads the smallest file that still looks sharp, with no layout shift.

sections.heading: The problem: one file cannot fit every screen
sections.body:
A CSS pixel is not a device pixel. A phone advertising a 360px-wide viewport may physically pack 1080 columns of hardware pixels into that width — a device pixel ratio (DPR) of 3. If you serve a 360px-wide image to that screen, the browser must stretch each image pixel across three hardware pixels and the result looks soft. To be sharp, the file needs roughly slot width times DPR real pixels.

The naive fix — ship everyone the biggest file — solves blur by creating a bandwidth disaster. A 1600px JPEG for a 360px slot on a 1x budget phone wastes around 90 percent of its bytes, slows the page, and costs users on metered connections real money. Neither a small file nor a big file is correct for everyone, because correctness depends on the visitor's screen and layout, which the server does not know when it writes the HTML.

The responsive images system inverts control: the HTML describes what files exist and how the image will be laid out, and the browser — the only party that knows the viewport, DPR, and even user preferences like data-saver mode — makes the final choice. Everything in this lesson is a way of feeding the browser that description.

sections.heading: Fixed-size images: srcset with x descriptors
sections.body:
When an image renders at a known, fixed CSS size — a 120px logo, a 48px avatar — the only variable is DPR, and x descriptors handle it directly. srcset lists alternative files, each tagged with the density it serves: logo.png 1x, logo@2x.png 2x, logo@3x.png 3x. A 2x screen picks the 2x file; a 1x screen downloads a quarter of the bytes for the same visual result.

The src attribute stays and acts as the 1x default plus the fallback for very old browsers, so you can safely omit an explicit 1x entry when src already points at the 1x file. The descriptors describe density only — the image still renders at whatever CSS size the layout gives it; the browser simply maps more file pixels onto each CSS pixel.

x descriptors are deliberately simple and deliberately limited: they assume the rendered size never changes. The moment an image's rendered width depends on the viewport — a hero, a card image in a fluid grid — density alone is not enough information, and you graduate to w descriptors.

sections.heading: Fluid images: srcset with w descriptors plus sizes
sections.body:
For images whose rendered width varies, srcset switches to w descriptors: each candidate is labeled with its true pixel width — hero-400.jpg 400w, hero-800.jpg 800w, hero-1600.jpg 1600w. The w number is a fact about the file, measured in real image pixels, and you should generate candidates at sensible intervals (commonly doubling, or steps of 300-400px) rather than one file per possible screen.

w descriptors alone are not enough, because the browser must choose a file before layout runs — before it knows how wide the image will render. The sizes attribute closes that gap by declaring the rendered width in advance as a list of media-condition and length pairs: sizes="(max-width: 600px) 100vw, 800px" means 'below 600px viewports this image spans the full viewport; otherwise it renders 800 CSS pixels wide'. The browser takes the first condition that matches; the final entry is the default and carries no condition.

The selection algorithm is then simple arithmetic: resolve sizes to a CSS width, multiply by DPR to get the needed pixel width, and download the smallest candidate at or above that number. A 360px viewport at DPR 3 needs about 1080 pixels, so it takes the 1600w file; the same viewport at DPR 1 takes the 400w file. Note that sizes is a promise, not a measurement — if it lies about the layout, the browser will faithfully fetch the wrong file, so update it when the CSS changes.

sections.heading: picture: art direction and format fallback
sections.body:
srcset always serves the same picture at different scales. The picture element handles the two cases where you need genuinely different files. It wraps one or more source elements followed by a required img: the browser walks the sources top to bottom, uses the first one whose media or type it accepts, and feeds its srcset into the img, which remains the element that actually renders (and carries alt, width, height and loading).

Art direction uses media attributes: on a wide screen you show the full landscape crop, but on a phone that crop shrinks the subject to a speck, so you swap in a tight square crop instead — <source media="(max-width: 600px)" srcset="hero-square.jpg">. Unlike sizes, which is advisory, a matching media on source is a command the browser must obey, because changing the crop is an editorial decision, not an optimization.

Format fallback uses type attributes with MIME types: list a modern, smaller format first and older fallbacks after — AVIF, then WebP, then the JPEG in the img src. A browser that cannot decode AVIF skips that source without downloading anything and tries the next. This is how you ship formats years before universal support: supporting browsers save 30-50 percent of bytes, everyone else silently gets the JPEG. The two mechanisms combine freely, and each source can carry its own w-descriptor srcset and sizes.

sections.heading: loading=lazy and decoding=async
sections.body:
loading="lazy" tells the browser not to fetch an image until the user scrolls near it. For a long page with twenty photos, that turns the initial load from twenty downloads into two or three, saving bandwidth for images many visitors never reach. The browser manages the distance threshold itself, typically starting the fetch a couple of viewport-heights early so the image is usually ready when it scrolls into view.

The critical exception is anything visible on first paint. Lazy-loading an above-the-fold hero actively hurts: the browser's preload scanner would normally start that download in the first milliseconds, but lazy loading forces it to wait for layout to confirm the position, delaying your Largest Contentful Paint. The rule is mechanical — first-screen images load eagerly (the default), everything below gets loading="lazy".

decoding="async" addresses a different cost: turning compressed bytes into pixels takes CPU time, and by default that decode can block the main thread alongside rendering. async gives the browser permission to decode off the critical path and paint the surrounding content first. It is a small, safe win for content images; the perceptible cases are large photos on modest devices.

sections.heading: width and height: the end of layout shift
sections.body:
Before an image downloads, the browser knows nothing about its shape and reserves zero height, so when the file arrives the whole page below it jumps — the classic layout shift that makes users tap the wrong link and tanks the Cumulative Layout Shift metric. The fix is the oldest pair of attributes in HTML: width and height, set to the image's intrinsic pixel dimensions.

Modern browsers use these two numbers to compute the aspect ratio immediately, and CSS like width: 100%; height: auto then scales the reserved box fluidly while keeping that ratio. The attribute values do not lock the rendered size — CSS still wins — they simply describe the image's shape so space can be reserved during the very first layout pass.

Write them as plain integers with no units, matching the real file (an 800×533 photo gets width="800" height="533"), and treat them as mandatory on every content image, including those inside picture. Combined with srcset for resolution, picture for format, and lazy loading for scheduling, dimensions complete the checklist for a professionally shipped image.

lessons.title: Make any page rank and preview correctly with head metadata
lessons.summary: Write the title, description, canonical, robots, Open Graph, Twitter card, JSON-LD and icon markup that search engines and social platforms actually read.
lessons.goal: Build a complete, production-grade head for an article page: search snippet, canonical URL, social link previews, structured data and icons.
lessons.whyItMatters: The head of a page is invisible to visitors but decides how the page appears everywhere else: the title and description shape its search listing, the canonical tag protects it from duplicate-content penalties, Open Graph and Twitter tags control the card people see when the link is shared in Slack, WhatsApp or X, and JSON-LD can earn rich results like star ratings and article cards. Teams routinely lose traffic to nothing more than a missing description or a broken og:image — this is cheap, high-impact markup every developer should be able to write from memory.
steps: Read the title and description section, then check the starter's title against the length guidance.
Add a meta description worth clicking (task 1).
Declare the canonical URL for the page (task 2).
Add the five core Open Graph tags that power link previews (task 3).
Add the Twitter card tag (task 4).
Add a JSON-LD script describing the article (task 5) and the icon links (task 6).
Press Run and confirm all six checks pass.
lessons.prompt:
<title>Roast coffee at home | BrewLab</title>
<meta name="description" content="A weekend guide to small-batch home roasting: gear, first crack, and the mistakes to skip.">
<link rel="canonical" href="https://brewlab.example/guides/home-roasting">
<meta property="og:title" content="Roast coffee at home">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://brewlab.example/img/roast-og.jpg">
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
lessons.explanation: The title is written page-topic-first with the brand after the separator, because search results truncate from the right. The meta description does not affect ranking directly but is the ad copy of the search listing, so it is a genuine sentence, not a keyword pile. The canonical link names the one official URL for this content, collapsing tracking-parameter and www/non-www duplicates into a single ranking target. The og:* tags feed link-preview scrapers, which never run JavaScript — they read exactly this markup and nothing else — and twitter:card selects the large-image layout on X.
lessons.example:
A marketing team shares their new guide in a customer Slack and the preview shows the bare domain, no image, and 'Untitled'. The scraper found no Open Graph tags and gave up.

After adding og:title, og:description, og:image (an absolute URL to a 1200×630 image), og:url and og:type, the same link unfurls into a full card with headline, blurb and photo — and click-through on shared links roughly doubles, with zero changes to the visible page.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, complete the head of the article page: meta description, canonical link, the five core og: properties, the twitter:card meta, a JSON-LD Article script, and the two icon links.
lessons.expectedResult: The visible preview shows only the article itself — every addition lives in the head — and all six checks pass in the console.
commonMistakes: Using a relative URL in og:image or canonical. Scrapers resolve nothing for you — both must be absolute URLs including the scheme and host.
Stuffing the title with keywords ('Coffee, roast coffee, home roasting, best roasting'). Search engines demote it and users distrust it; write one clear phrase plus the brand.
Adding noindex to a page and forgetting it after launch. A single leftover robots meta can silently remove a production page from search for months.
Duplicating the same title and description across every page of a site. Each page competes for different queries and needs its own pair.
lessons.proTip: Every major platform has a debugger that shows you exactly what its scraper sees — search for 'Facebook Sharing Debugger', 'LinkedIn Post Inspector' or 'Twitter Card Validator'. They also force a re-scrape, which is how you fix a stale preview after correcting your tags.

coding.intro: You will finish the head of an article page so that search engines index it correctly and chat apps unfurl it into a rich preview card.

sections.heading: title and meta description: your search listing
sections.body:
The title element does double duty: it labels the browser tab and becomes the blue headline of your search result. Aim for roughly 50-60 characters — longer titles get cut off with an ellipsis — and put the page's specific topic first, the site brand last, separated by a pipe or dash: 'Roast coffee at home | BrewLab'. Front-loading matters because truncation eats the end, and because scanners read the first words only. Every page needs a unique title; templates that produce the same title sitewide throw away the strongest on-page signal search engines have.

The meta description — <meta name="description" content="…"> — supplies the grey snippet under that headline. It is not a ranking factor, but it is the difference between being seen and being clicked: write one or two real sentences, around 150-160 characters, that tell the searcher what they will get and why this page answers their query. Think of it as ad copy that must be honest.

Search engines treat the description as a suggestion, not a contract: if it is missing, spammy, or does not match the query, they will synthesize a snippet from page text instead. That fallback is usually worse than what you would write, which is the practical argument for authoring one on every indexable page.
sections.code:
<title>Roast coffee at home | BrewLab</title>
<meta name="description" content="A weekend guide to small-batch home roasting: the gear that matters, hearing first crack, and the three mistakes every beginner makes.">

sections.heading: rel=canonical: one official URL per page
sections.body:
The same content is usually reachable at many URLs: with and without www, with tracking parameters (?utm_source=newsletter), with trailing-slash variants, sometimes on both http and https. To a search engine each variant is a separate page, so your ranking signals get split across duplicates and the engine must guess which one to show. The canonical link ends the guessing: <link rel="canonical" href="…"> declares the one URL you consider official for this content.

Every indexable page should carry a canonical, even when no duplicates exist yet — a self-referencing canonical is standard practice because duplicates tend to appear later through campaign links and syndication. The href must be absolute (scheme and host included) and should point at the clean, parameter-free form of the URL. When another site republishes your article, their copy can canonical back to yours, passing the credit home.

Canonical is advisory but strongly respected; the related robots meta is a directive. <meta name="robots" content="noindex"> orders engines to keep the page out of results entirely — right for staging sites, thin search-results pages and thank-you pages. nofollow additionally tells them not to pass credit through the page's links. The operational hazard runs in both directions: forgetting noindex leaks staging into Google, and shipping a leftover noindex to production silently deletes a live page from search, so many teams add an automated check for exactly this tag.
sections.code:
<link rel="canonical" href="https://brewlab.example/guides/home-roasting">

<!-- keep this page out of search results entirely -->
<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">

sections.heading: Open Graph: how link previews are built
sections.body:
When someone pastes your URL into Slack, WhatsApp, LinkedIn or iMessage, the platform's scraper fetches the page once and builds the preview card entirely from meta tags in the head. The vocabulary those scrapers share is Open Graph — meta elements using property (not name) attributes with the og: prefix. No tags, no card: the platform falls back to a bare domain or guesses badly.

Five properties cover almost every case. og:title is the card headline — often shorter and punchier than the SEO title, with no brand suffix. og:description is the one-to-two line teaser. og:image is the picture, and it is the tag that breaks most often: it must be an absolute URL, and the near-universal sweet spot is a 1200×630 image (a 1.91:1 ratio) so it fills the large-card crop on every platform. og:url states the canonical URL of the content, keeping share counts consolidated. og:type describes what the thing is — website for most pages, article for posts and guides, plus niche types like video.other.

One operational fact explains most preview bugs: scrapers do not execute JavaScript, and most platforms cache the first scrape aggressively. Tags injected client-side by a SPA framework are invisible to them — Open Graph markup must be present in the server-rendered HTML — and after you fix a tag you must force a re-scrape with the platform's debugger tool to evict the cached card.
sections.code:
<meta property="og:title" content="Roast coffee at home">
<meta property="og:description" content="Gear, first crack, and the mistakes to skip — a weekend guide.">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://brewlab.example/img/roast-og.jpg">
<meta property="og:url" content="https://brewlab.example/guides/home-roasting">
<meta property="og:type" content="article">

sections.heading: Twitter cards: the one extra tag that matters
sections.body:
X (Twitter) reads Open Graph tags as its fallback, so you do not duplicate everything — but it has its own switch for the card layout. <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image"> selects the full-width image card that dominates timelines; the alternative value summary produces a small square thumbnail beside the text. Note the attribute difference: Twitter's vocabulary uses name, while Open Graph uses property — mixing them up is the classic silent failure, because the scraper simply ignores tags with the wrong attribute.

The optional twitter:site tag credits the site's account (content="@brewlab") and twitter:creator credits the individual author, which attaches attribution to the card. If you provide twitter:title, twitter:description or twitter:image they override the og: equivalents on X only — useful when you want platform-specific copy, ignorable otherwise.

The pragmatic recipe for a content site is therefore: full og: set, plus twitter:card, plus twitter:site if the brand has an account. That combination renders correctly on effectively every platform that unfurls links today.
sections.code:
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
<meta name="twitter:site" content="@brewlab">

sections.heading: Structured data: JSON-LD in one section
sections.body:
Beyond previews, search engines want machine-readable facts about a page — who wrote the article and when, what a recipe's rating is, what a product costs. The format they recommend is JSON-LD: a script element with type="application/ld+json" containing a JSON object that uses the schema.org vocabulary. Because the type is not JavaScript, browsers never execute it; it is pure data riding inside the HTML.

The object declares @context (always https://schema.org), an @type such as Article, Product, Recipe, FAQPage or LocalBusiness, and the properties that type defines. Accurate structured data is what makes pages eligible for rich results — the star ratings, prices, FAQ dropdowns and article carousels that occupy the best real estate on a results page. Eligibility is the honest word: engines choose when to show rich results, and they penalize markup that claims things the visible page does not contain.

For a working developer the awareness level is: know the format, keep the JSON valid (one syntax error invalidates the whole block), mirror only facts that are visibly on the page, and validate with Google's Rich Results Test. Deep schema modeling is a specialty of its own; the entry ticket is this one script element done correctly.
sections.code:
<script type="application/ld+json">
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "Article",
  "headline": "Roast coffee at home",
  "author": { "@type": "Person", "name": "Dana Petrou" },
  "datePublished": "2026-08-01"
}
</script>

sections.heading: Icons: favicon and apple-touch-icon
sections.body:
Icons are metadata too, and browser tabs, bookmark lists, phone home screens and search results all draw from the link elements in your head. The modern minimal set is two lines. First, a standard icon: <link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml"> — SVG scales to every size from a 16px tab to a large bookmark tile, and browsers that predate SVG favicons still fall back to requesting /favicon.ico from the site root, so keeping that legacy file in place costs nothing and covers ancient clients.

Second, the Apple touch icon: <link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">. iOS uses it when someone adds the page to their home screen, and expects a 180×180 PNG with no transparency — iOS composites its own rounded corners. Several Android browsers and various chat apps also read this tag as a high-resolution icon source, which is why it belongs on every site, Apple-focused or not.

Sites that behave as installable apps add a web app manifest (<link rel="manifest" href="/site.webmanifest">) which lists further icon sizes for install surfaces. For an ordinary content site, the SVG icon, the legacy favicon.ico and the apple-touch-icon are the complete, modern answer — the sprawling twenty-line icon blocks old generators produced are obsolete.
sections.code:
<link rel="icon" href="/icon.svg" type="image/svg+xml">
<link rel="apple-touch-icon" href="/apple-touch-icon.png">
<!-- /favicon.ico kept at the site root as the silent fallback -->

lessons.title: Ship pages every user can read: alt text, outlines and skip links
lessons.summary: Treat accessibility as a requirement: master the four kinds of alt text, audit heading outlines and landmarks, add a skip link, and own contrast and language correctness.
lessons.goal: Repair an article page so screen-reader users get real image descriptions, a working outline, a skip link and correct language information.
lessons.whyItMatters: Roughly one in six people has a disability that affects how they use the web, and in a growing number of jurisdictions inaccessible sites are a legal liability, not just a quality gap. Most accessibility failures are not exotic — audits keep finding the same basics: missing alt text, broken heading outlines, no way to skip repeated navigation, illegible contrast. These are HTML-level decisions made by whoever writes the markup, which means the developer either builds accessibility in or builds the barrier in. This lesson makes the basics automatic.
steps: Read the framing section: accessibility is an engineering requirement with a standard (WCAG), not a polish step.
Write an informative alt for the photo (task 1) and an empty alt for the decorative divider (task 2).
Add the skip link at the top of the body (task 3) and give main the matching id (task 4).
Repair the heading outline: the section titles were chosen for size, not level (task 5).
Declare the document language (task 6).
Press Run, confirm all checks pass, then Tab through the preview to feel the skip link work.
lessons.prompt:
Skip to content …

Watching the spring migration

Where to stand
lessons.explanation: The skip link is the first focusable element on the page, so a keyboard user's very first Tab press offers a shortcut past the navigation; it targets the id on main. The photo's alt conveys what the image contributes — the scale and behavior of the flock — rather than restating 'photo of birds'. The divider image is decoration, so alt="" tells screen readers to skip it silently instead of announcing a meaningless filename. Together with a sequential heading outline, these give a non-visual reader the same structure a sighted reader gets by glancing.
lessons.example:
A screen-reader user opens the article and hears: 'graphic flock underscore final underscore v2 dot jpg' — the filename, because alt is missing — then must arrow through forty navigation links to reach the text, and the section list is meaningless because every heading is an h4.

After the repair, the same user hears a real description of the photo, jumps straight to the content with the skip link, and pulls up a headings list that reads like a table of contents.
lessons.exercise: In the editor on the right, fix the article: informative alt on the photo, empty alt on the decorative divider, a skip link wired to main, section headings promoted to their correct level, and lang on the html element.
lessons.expectedResult: The preview looks nearly identical — one hidden link appears on first Tab — but the underlying page now works for keyboard and screen-reader users, and all six checks pass.
commonMistakes: Starting alt text with 'Image of' or 'Photo of'. Screen readers already announce the element as a graphic, so the phrase is pure noise — describe the content directly.
Omitting alt entirely instead of writing alt="". Missing alt makes screen readers fall back to the filename; the empty string is an explicit, meaningful signal to skip.
Choosing heading levels for their default font size. Levels are structure; if h2 looks too big, restyle it with CSS.
Hiding the skip link with display: none. That removes it from the Tab order entirely — hide it off-screen and reveal it on :focus instead.
lessons.proTip: The fastest audit you can run: press Tab from the address bar and watch where focus goes, then open the accessibility tree in DevTools (or a headings list in a screen reader) and read your outline. Five minutes, and it catches the majority of the failures in this lesson.

coding.intro: You will repair a bird-watching article that fails four basic accessibility checks: image descriptions, document outline, skip navigation and language.

sections.heading: A requirement, not a feature
sections.body:
Accessibility is the property of a page being usable by people regardless of how they perceive and operate it: through a screen reader, by keyboard alone, with magnification, with limited color perception, with a tremor that makes small targets hard to hit. It is not an optional enhancement layer — it is part of the definition of 'working', the same way security is. A checkout that blind users cannot complete is broken, whether or not anyone on the team noticed.

The standard that defines 'accessible' in practice is WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines), whose success criteria are organized in levels; level AA is the common legal and contractual target, referenced by regulations like the European Accessibility Act and by most procurement requirements. You do not need to memorize the document — you need the habits it encodes, and the ones in this lesson cover a remarkable share of real-world failures.

The economic framing matters too: the fixes below are nearly free at authoring time and expensive to retrofit at audit time. Alt text, correct heading levels, a skip link and a lang attribute add minutes to a page's construction. The same items found in a compliance audit two years later mean re-opening hundreds of templates. Accessibility done as a requirement is cheap; done as a remediation project it never is.
sections.code:
<!-- the deliverable is not 'a page that looks right' —
     it is 'a page that works through eyes, ears or keyboard' -->

sections.heading: Informative images: alt that carries the meaning
sections.body:
The alt attribute is the text that replaces an image when the image cannot be seen — read aloud by screen readers, shown when the file fails to load, indexed by search engines. Writing it well starts with one question: what does this image contribute here? The answer, phrased as if you were reading the page to someone over the phone, is the alt text.

For an informative image, describe the relevant content, not the medium. alt="Hundreds of storks circling a thermal above the ridge" carries the article's point; alt="image" or the filename carries nothing, and prefixes like 'Photo of' are redundant because the screen reader already announces it as a graphic. Keep it roughly a sentence — alt is a replacement, not a caption, and it should be as long as necessary and no longer.

Context changes the correct answer for the identical file. A portrait on a team page might be alt="Dana Petrou", while the same portrait illustrating an article about studio lighting might be alt="Portrait lit by a single soft key light from the left". There is no universally right alt for an image, only a right alt for an image in a context — which is why it cannot be autogenerated well and belongs to whoever writes the page.

sections.heading: Functional, decorative and complex images
sections.body:
When an image is interactive — a logo that links home, an icon that submits a search — its alt must state the function, not the appearance: alt="BrewLab home", alt="Search". The screen-reader user is deciding whether to activate it, and 'magnifying glass icon' answers the wrong question.

Purely decorative images — dividers, background flourishes, stock art that adds mood but no information — get the explicit empty string: alt="". This is a deliberate signal meaning 'nothing to say here; skip silently', and it is completely different from omitting the attribute, which forces screen readers to guess and usually ends with the filename being read aloud. Every img needs an alt attribute; the empty value is one of its legitimate values. (Decoration is often better delivered as CSS background-image, which needs no alt at all.)

Complex images — charts, diagrams, maps — cannot be compressed into one alt sentence. The pattern is a short alt naming the image plus its conclusion ('Bar chart: signups doubled after the March launch') with the full data available to everyone nearby: a table below the chart, a details element with the description, or a link to it. figure with figcaption pairs the image with a visible caption, but note the caption and the alt have different jobs — the caption comments, the alt replaces — so a figcaption does not excuse an empty alt on an informative image.

sections.heading: Landmarks and the heading outline
sections.body:
Screen readers navigate structurally: users pull up a list of landmarks or headings and jump, rather than reading linearly. Landmarks come from the sectioning elements you already know — header, nav, main, aside, footer — and the two rules that matter are: exactly one main per page, and a label (aria-label) on any landmark that appears twice, so 'navigation' and 'navigation' become 'primary' and 'breadcrumb'.

The heading outline is the finer-grained map. Audit it by reading only the headings top to bottom: one h1 stating what the page is, h2 for each major section, h3 nested inside an h2's territory, never skipping levels going down. The audit fails in predictable ways — multiple h1s from a template collision, an h4 chosen because its default size looked right, bold paragraphs acting as fake headings that appear in nobody's headings list.

The fix is always the same: assign the level the structure demands and move appearance to CSS. This is the single highest-value habit in the lesson, because the headings list is to a screen-reader user what the visual layout is to everyone else — the primary way of understanding what the page contains and getting to the wanted part.

sections.heading: The skip link
sections.body:
Sighted mouse users ignore repeated page furniture and click straight into content. A keyboard user has no such shortcut: every page of your site makes them Tab through the same logo, navigation and search box before reaching the article — potentially dozens of presses, on every single page. The skip link is the standard remedy: the first focusable element in the body is a link reading 'Skip to content' whose href targets the main element's id.

Activating it moves focus past the repeated header, and because main is not natively focusable, robust implementations add tabindex="-1" to it so every browser reliably moves both focus and reading position. The link itself is usually hidden until needed: positioned off-screen by default and brought into view by a :focus rule. Never hide it with display: none or the hidden attribute — both remove it from the Tab order, which deletes the feature while leaving the markup.

A skip link costs three lines and is one of the most-used accessibility features in existence — it also helps sighted keyboard users, switch users, and anyone on a screen magnifier. WCAG requires a mechanism to bypass repeated blocks; this is the canonical one.

sections.heading: Contrast and language: two responsibilities you own
sections.body:
Color contrast is decided wherever colors are chosen, and WCAG AA sets the floor: a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 between text and its background for normal text, relaxed to 3:1 for large text (roughly 24px, or 19px bold). The fashionable light-grey-on-white caption at 2.4:1 fails — not just for low-vision users, but for anyone reading a phone in sunlight. Every browser's DevTools shows the ratio when you inspect a color, and design tools flag it too; checking costs seconds. The related rule: color can never be the only carrier of information — an error state shown purely by a red border disappears for a colorblind user, so pair it with text or an icon.

Language correctness is the other quiet responsibility. lang="en" on the html element selects the screen reader's pronunciation engine, the browser's hyphenation rules and the spellchecker's dictionary; without it, software guesses, and an English voice reading French produces gibberish. Mark inline language switches on the smallest containing element — a quoted sentence, a foreign title — and keep the tag truthful: a template hardcoding lang="en" on a German site is an accessibility bug that affects every sentence of every page.

Neither of these appears in a visual review. Both are caught in seconds by the habits this lesson builds — which is the general shape of accessibility work: not harder, just deliberate.

A developer who knows both the attributes and the restraint to prefer native HTML is exactly what teams need.

sections.heading: What ARIA is, and its first rule
sections.body:
ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes that change how elements are described to assistive technology. It edits the accessibility tree — the parallel structure screen readers consume — and only that. This is the most important mechanical fact about ARIA: it changes announcements, never behavior. role="button" makes a div claim to be a button; it does not make Enter or Space activate it, does not make it focusable, does not give it a disabled state. Every promise ARIA makes, your JavaScript must keep.

That is why the specification's own first rule of ARIA is: do not use ARIA if a native HTML element or attribute already provides the semantics and behavior. <button> beats role="button" because it brings focus, key handling, form participation and disabled state for free. <nav> beats role="navigation". checked beats aria-checked on a real checkbox. Native elements are tested implementations; ARIA on generic elements is a claim you must back with code.

The corollary rules matter too: do not change native semantics (no role="tab" on an h2 — put the role on a wrapper), all interactive ARIA widgets must be keyboard-operable, and never put role="presentation" or aria-hidden="true" on a focusable element. ARIA earns its keep in the gaps — states like expanded, relationships between elements, live announcements — which the rest of this lesson covers.

sections.heading: role: what an element claims to be
sections.body:
The role attribute assigns an element a slot in the accessibility taxonomy. Most elements have an implicit role already — button is button, a[href] is link, nav is navigation, input type="checkbox" is checkbox — and DevTools' accessibility panel shows the computed role for anything you select. Explicit role exists for elements that have no useful implicit role (usually div and span pressed into service as widgets) and for the rare cases where you must repurpose an element.

The roles you will actually reach for fall into groups. Landmark roles (banner, navigation, main, complementary, contentinfo) mirror header, nav, main, aside and footer — use the elements, not the roles, in new code. Widget roles describe interactive patterns: tab, tablist and tabpanel for tab interfaces, dialog for overlays, switch for on/off toggles, menu strictly for application-style menus (not site navigation — a common and harmful mix-up, since role="menu" makes screen readers expect arrow-key behavior). Structural roles like list, listitem, img and presentation describe non-interactive content; role="presentation" strips semantics from an element whose markup is purely layout.

Two standing warnings. First, a role is a contract: role="tab" obliges you to implement arrow-key movement, aria-selected state and focus management, because users will drive it with the keys that pattern promises. Second, never write a role that contradicts behavior — an element that claims to be a checkbox but only responds to hover is a trap for exactly the users the attribute was meant to help.

sections.heading: Naming: aria-label vs aria-labelledby vs aria-describedby
sections.body:
Every interactive element needs an accessible name — the word or phrase a screen reader says to identify it. Native mechanisms come first: a button's text content, an img's alt, a form field's label element. ARIA offers three attributes for when those are not enough, and they are not interchangeable.

aria-label supplies the name directly as a string. It is the tool for elements whose visible content does not name them: an icon-only close button (aria-label="Close"), or one nav among several (aria-label="Primary" — the label is announced together with the role, as 'Primary navigation'). Its weaknesses: it is invisible, so it silently drifts out of date, and it is not translated by most machine-translation tools. It also overrides the element's content entirely — an aria-label on a button replaces the button's text in announcements, a frequent source of mislabeled controls.

aria-labelledby points at the id of one or more elements whose visible text already names the thing — a section labeled by its own heading is the canonical case. Because the name is on-screen text, it cannot drift and it does get translated; when both are present, labelledby beats label. aria-describedby is different in kind: it attaches supplementary description, announced after the name, typically for hint text or error messages tied to an input. Name answers 'what is this?'; description answers 'what else should I know?' — keep the name short and push detail into the description.

sections.heading: aria-hidden: removing noise
sections.body:
aria-hidden="true" removes an element and its entire subtree from the accessibility tree while leaving it visually present — the mirror image of a visually-hidden CSS class, which hides from sight but keeps the announcement. Its everyday job is decorative noise: an icon sitting next to its own text label would otherwise be announced twice or read as a cryptic character, so the icon gets aria-hidden="true" and the text carries the meaning.

The safety rule is absolute: never aria-hide anything focusable, or any container holding something focusable. The element stays in the Tab order, so a keyboard-using screen-reader user lands on a control that, per the accessibility tree, does not exist — focus announces nothing, and the user is stranded. If content must be hidden from everyone, use the hidden attribute or display: none, both of which also remove focusability; aria-hidden is only for the narrow case of 'visible, but silent'.

Note the inverse does not exist: aria-hidden="false" does not force-reveal content inside a hidden subtree, and sprinkling it around is a no-op that signals confusion. Also resist aria-hiding real content like images with meaning — that is what empty alt is for on images, and content that informs sighted users almost always informs everyone.

sections.heading: Disclosure widgets: aria-expanded and aria-controls
sections.body:
The disclosure — a button that shows and hides a panel — is the most common interactive pattern on the web: dropdown menus, mobile burgers, accordions, 'show more' toggles. Its accessible form is compact: a native button carrying aria-expanded, plus the panel it toggles. aria-expanded="false" makes the screen reader announce 'Menu, button, collapsed'; when script opens the panel it must also set aria-expanded="true", and the announcement becomes 'expanded'. The attribute lives on the button (the thing the user is on), never on the panel, and its value must be updated by the same code path that toggles visibility — a static aria-expanded is a lie in markup form.

aria-controls="panel-id" records which element the button drives. Its practical value is modest — some screen readers offer a jump-to-controlled-element command, and it serves as machine-readable documentation — but it costs one attribute and completes the pattern. The panel itself needs no ARIA: its visibility is handled by hidden, which removes it from both sight and the accessibility tree in one move.

Before building this by hand, remember the native option: details/summary implements a disclosure with zero JavaScript and correct announcements built in. The manual pattern earns its place when design or behavior requirements outgrow details — which is the first rule of ARIA applied at the widget level.

sections.heading: Live regions: announcing what changed
sections.body:
Screen readers narrate where the user's focus is. When JavaScript changes content elsewhere — 'Saved', '3 results found', 'Connection lost' — nothing is announced, because the user never visited that spot. Live regions fix this: an element marked aria-live tells assistive technology to watch it and announce whatever text appears inside. aria-live="polite" queues the announcement until the user pauses — right for nearly everything: status updates, result counts, autosave confirmations. aria-live="assertive" interrupts the user mid-word and is reserved for genuinely urgent information such as session-expiry warnings; overusing it trains users to resent your product. Two shorthand roles bundle these semantics: role="status" implies polite, role="alert" implies assertive, and both are widely supported. The implementation detail that catches everyone: the live region must exist in the DOM, empty, from page load. Screen readers register regions when they first build the tree, so creating the element and its message in the same script tick frequently goes unannounced. The robust pattern is a permanent empty container —

— whose textContent your script updates. Keep messages short and self-contained ('Draft saved at 14:02'), because the user hears them without any surrounding context.

lessons.whyItMatters: Keyboard access is the load-bearing wall of accessibility: screen-reader users, switch users, people with motor impairments and plenty of power users all drive the web without a mouse. It is also where the most common self-inflicted wounds live — clickable divs that Tab skips entirely, outline: none shipped because a designer disliked the focus ring, positive tabindex values that scramble the order. Every one of these makes parts of an interface literally unreachable for some users, and every one has a small, standard fix.

sections.heading: The keyboard model
sections.body:
Keyboard navigation runs on a handful of conventions every user relies on. Tab moves focus forward through the page's interactive elements; Shift+Tab moves backward. Enter activates links and buttons; Space also activates buttons (and scrolls the page otherwise); arrow keys move within composite widgets like radio groups, select menus and tab bars; Escape dismisses overlays. Focus is the keyboard's cursor — exactly one element holds it at a time, and everything the user does happens there.

The set of elements Tab visits is the tab order, and by default it contains only interactive elements: links with href, buttons, form fields, summary, and a few others. Plain divs, spans, paragraphs and images are not focusable — which is correct, because a Tab stop that does nothing wastes the user's time. This default is well-calibrated: most pages need no tabindex anywhere, because using native interactive elements produces the right tab order automatically.

Who depends on this? Blind users, whose screen readers are driven from the keyboard. People with tremors or limited fine motor control, for whom precise pointing is exhausting. Switch-access users, whose entire input may be one or two buttons. Power users filling forms. Anyone whose trackpad died on a deadline. Keyboard support is not an edge case — it is a parallel, fully load-bearing input channel.

A side note on HTML's built-in shortcut attribute: accesskey assigns a single-character shortcut to an element, and in practice it is avoided. The activating modifier differs per browser and OS, the shortcuts are undiscoverable, and the chosen letters collide with browser and screen-reader commands — hijacking keys from the very users who live on the keyboard. Application shortcuts belong in JavaScript with a visible cheat sheet, not in accesskey.

sections.heading: Tab order comes from source order
sections.body:
The natural tab order is simply document order: the browser walks the DOM top to bottom and visits each focusable element as it appears in the markup. This has a powerful consequence — if your HTML is written in reading order, keyboard navigation is correct by construction, with zero attributes.

It also has a trap. CSS can reorder things visually — flexbox order, grid placement, absolute positioning — without changing the DOM, so a layout that shows the primary action on the left may still Tab to it last because it comes last in the source. The user watches focus jump diagonally across the screen. The fix is never to patch with tabindex numbers; it is to reorder the source so DOM order and visual order agree, and to treat large divergences between them as a design smell.

When auditing, remember disabled controls leave the tab order entirely, and elements hidden with display: none, the hidden attribute, or inert subtrees are unfocusable. Off-screen-positioned content, however, remains focusable — the cause of the classic bug where Tab visits an invisible closed menu. Anything visually hidden but still in the DOM must either be truly hidden or be intended to take focus (like a skip link that reveals itself on focus).

sections.heading: tabindex: the two useful values
sections.body:
tabindex="0" adds an element to the natural tab order at its source position. Its legitimate use is narrow: custom interactive widgets that cannot be built from native elements — a canvas-based editor, a div acting as a slider — where you are hand-implementing interactivity. Adding it to non-interactive content is an anti-pattern: a focusable paragraph is a stop that does nothing, and screen-reader users can already read text without it being focusable.

tabindex="-1" makes an element focusable only programmatically: Tab skips it, but element.focus() works. This is the workhorse of focus management — the technique of moving focus deliberately when the interface changes context. Route focus to an error summary after failed validation, to the heading of a newly revealed panel, to the first field of a dialog, back to the triggering button when the dialog closes. Every single-page-app navigation should move focus to the new content's container, and tabindex="-1" is what makes those targets focusable.

Positive values (tabindex="1" and above) build a priority queue the browser visits before every normally focusable element, in ascending numeric order, wherever those elements sit on the page. The result is an order maintained by hand, invisible in the markup's flow, broken by the next refactor. There is no modern use case; every problem positive tabindex appears to solve is solved better by reordering source. Treat any positive value in review as a bug.

sections.heading: Focus must be visible: :focus-visible
sections.body:
A keyboard user's focus ring is their mouse cursor: without it they are navigating blind, counting Tab presses and guessing. That is why WCAG requires visible focus indication, and why the once-ubiquitous outline: none with no replacement is among the most harmful lines of CSS ever popularized. The motivation was real — clicking a button also focuses it, and designers hated the ring flashing on every mouse click — but the cure disabled navigation for keyboard users to tidy up aesthetics for mouse users.

:focus-visible resolves the conflict. The plain :focus pseudo-class matches whenever the element has focus, regardless of input; :focus-visible matches only when the browser judges the indicator should be shown — in practice, keyboard and other non-pointer interaction. Style :focus-visible with a strong ring and mouse clicks stay clean while Tab navigation lights up exactly as it should. A good default ring is a 2px solid outline in a high-contrast color with outline-offset for breathing room; outline is the right property because, unlike border, it occupies no layout space.

If a legacy stylesheet already nukes outlines, the repair is to add the :focus-visible rule rather than hunting every reset — and going forward, the rule of review is simple: no outline: none without a :focus-visible replacement in the same change.

sections.heading: The sr-only pattern: visible to ears, not eyes
sections.body:
Icon-only controls are everywhere — a B for bold, a trash can, a gear — and each one needs a text name for users who cannot see the icon. One approach is aria-label on the button. The other is the sr-only (screen-reader-only) CSS class: a span of real text hidden visually but left in the accessibility tree, paired with the icon marked aria-hidden="true".

The class works by shrinking the element to a 1px clipped box and removing it from flow: position absolute, 1px width and height, clip-path or clip to hide the pixel, overflow hidden, white-space nowrap to stop reflow tricks. What it deliberately avoids is display: none and visibility: hidden — both of those remove content from screen readers too, which is the opposite of the goal. The standard rule has been battle-tested for a decade; copy it, do not improvise it.

sr-only text has advantages over aria-label worth knowing: it is real content, so it is picked up by translation tools, by find-in-page in some contexts, and by any code reading textContent; and it works on elements where aria-label support is shaky. It is also the mechanism behind skip links (sr-only until focused, then revealed) and behind extra context for screen readers like a 'Read more' link followed by an sr-only 'about the spring migration'. Keep it for short functional text — hiding entire paragraphs of alternate content quickly drifts out of sync with the visible page.

sections.heading: The clickable div, done right — and why button still wins
sections.body:
A div with a click handler looks identical to a button and fails every non-mouse test: Tab skips it, Enter and Space do nothing, screen readers announce it as plain text, and it has no disabled semantics. Making it genuinely equivalent takes four additions: role="button" so it announces correctly; tabindex="0" so Tab reaches it; a keydown handler that activates on both Enter and Space (and prevents Space's default page scroll); and focus styling via the :focus-visible rule. Miss any one and some users get a broken control.

Write that list out and the conclusion writes itself: <button> ships all four, plus form participation, plus a real disabled state, plus correct behavior in edge cases you have not thought of, in tested browser code. The div version is four requirements you must implement, review and maintain forever. 'We can make the div accessible' is true and beside the point — the button is the same work already done.

The honest reasons a div survives are styling habits (fixed by a two-line CSS reset for buttons) and framework inertia. The honest exceptions are components that genuinely are not buttons — complex composite widgets with their own interaction grammar. For anything that is pressed to make one thing happen, the professional default is the native element; reach for the ARIA-and-tabindex kit only when you can say precisely why button cannot work.

lessons.title: Build accordions, modals and popovers with native HTML
lessons.summary: Use details/summary for disclosures and exclusive accordions, the dialog element for modals with method="dialog" forms, and the popover attribute for lightweight overlays — no JavaScript frameworks required.
lessons.goal: Build a help center with a native FAQ accordion, a confirmation dialog and a keyboard-shortcuts popover.
lessons.whyItMatters: Accordions, modals and tooltips used to mean pulling in a component library and hand-wiring focus traps, Escape handling and ARIA state. HTML now ships all three patterns natively: details/summary has been solid for years, dialog gives you real modality with a browser-managed backdrop, and the popover attribute covers light-dismiss overlays with zero script for the open/close plumbing. Knowing these primitives means shipping less JavaScript, fewer accessibility bugs, and interfaces that keep working when scripts fail — and knowing which primitive fits which job is the actual senior skill.

Open the first FAQ item by default with the open attribute (task 3).
Read the dialog section, then add the confirmation dialog with its method="dialog" form (task 4).
Read the popover section, then add the shortcuts popover (task 5) and wire the button to it with popovertarget (task 6).

The native version is one details element per question. Keyboard toggling, screen-reader announcements and state management are browser code, find-in-page can even auto-expand matching items in Chromium, and the JavaScript budget for the feature is zero.

commonMistakes: Putting the whole answer inside summary. Only the toggle line belongs there; the collapsible content comes after it, still inside details.
Showing a modal by adding the open attribute instead of calling showModal(). The attribute route gives a non-modal box: no backdrop, no focus trap, no Escape handling.
Nesting interactive controls inside summary — a link inside the toggle makes every click a gamble between following the link and toggling the disclosure.
Reaching for dialog when a popover fits (or vice versa): if the user must respond before continuing, it is a modal dialog; if clicking elsewhere should simply dismiss it, it is a popover.
