coding.intro: You will build a help center from three native disclosure primitives: a details-based FAQ accordion, a dialog for confirmation, and a popover for keyboard shortcuts.

sections.heading: details and summary: disclosure without JavaScript
sections.body:
The details element is a built-in disclosure widget. Its first summary child is the permanently visible header; every other child is hidden until the widget opens. Clicking the summary — or focusing it and pressing Enter or Space — toggles the state, and the browser handles focusability, announcements ('button, collapsed'), and state management with no attributes and no script.

The open attribute reflects and controls the state. Author it in the markup to render a details expanded from the start — the right call for the most-asked question in an FAQ or the currently relevant section of documentation. It is also a live attribute: the browser adds and removes it as the user toggles, scripts can set el.open = true, and CSS can target the expanded state with details[open], which is how a custom chevron gets its rotation.

Styling notes worth knowing: the summary displays a disclosure triangle via its ::marker pseudo-element, removable with summary::marker { content: '' } (WebKit historically needed summary::-webkit-details-marker { display: none }). The hidden content is genuinely absent from rendering and the accessibility tree while closed — though Chromium's find-in-page can search closed details and auto-expand the match, a free feature hand-rolled accordions rarely replicate. Keep summary content simple text: interactive elements inside it fight the toggle for clicks.

sections.heading: Exclusive accordions with the name attribute
sections.body:
A classic accordion allows only one panel open at a time — historically the point where developers gave up on details and wrote JavaScript to close the siblings. The name attribute removed that last excuse: give several details elements the same name, exactly like radio buttons sharing a group, and the browser enforces exclusivity. Opening any member automatically closes whichever other member was open.

The group is defined purely by the shared name value; the elements do not need to be siblings or share a parent, though an accordion almost always renders them as a stacked list. At most one member of a named group can carry the open attribute in markup — authoring two as open is invalid, and the browser resolves the conflict by keeping only the first open.

One design caution before making every FAQ exclusive: exclusivity is sometimes hostile. A user comparing two answers cannot see both at once, and opening a lower item collapses an upper one, jolting the scroll position. Reserve name-grouping for genuinely either/or content — steps of a wizard-like flow, settings categories — and let independent details stand alone when users may want several open. The feature also degrades gracefully: browsers that predate name simply treat the group as independent disclosures, losing only the exclusivity.

sections.heading: dialog: open vs showModal()
sections.body:
The dialog element is a box for conversations that interrupt the page — confirmations, forms, pickers. It renders nothing by default, and the way you show it decides what kind of thing it is. Calling dialog.show() (or authoring the open attribute) presents it non-modally: visible, but the rest of the page stays interactive behind it, like a chat panel or a toast with actions.

Calling dialog.showModal() presents it modally, and the browser takes over the hard parts that made hand-rolled modals infamous: the page behind becomes inert — unclickable, unfocusable, unreachable by Tab, hidden from screen readers; focus moves into the dialog and is trapped there; Escape closes it; and it renders in the top layer, above every z-index in the document, with a companion ::backdrop pseudo-element you can style into the classic dimmed overlay. Every one of those bullet points was previously a category of accessibility bug.

The practical rules: never author the open attribute for a modal — attribute-opened dialogs are always non-modal, so the markup ships the element closed and script calls showModal(). When the dialog opens, focus goes to the first focusable element inside, overridable by putting autofocus on whichever control should receive it — usually the safe action in a destructive confirmation. And when the dialog closes, browsers return focus to the element that opened it, completing the loop keyboard users depend on.

sections.heading: method="dialog": forms that close the dialog
sections.body:
A form inside a dialog can set method="dialog", a special method that submits nowhere. Instead, submitting closes the dialog and sets the dialog's returnValue property to the value attribute of the button that submitted. Two buttons — Cancel with value="cancel", Delete with value="delete" — thus close the dialog through the same native path, and the script that opened it reads which choice was made in the dialog's close event.

This inverts the usual wiring. Without method="dialog" you attach click handlers to every button, call close() manually, and track the outcome in your own variables. With it, the buttons need no JavaScript at all: the form is the state machine, Escape still works and reports an empty returnValue, and the dialog behaves identically whether the user clicks, presses Enter on a focused button, or dismisses. Pairing autofocus onto the non-destructive button completes a confirmation pattern that is safe by default.

Two footnotes for completeness: a plain button inside a form defaults to type="submit", which is why both buttons close the dialog — a button that must not close it needs type="button". And the newer closedby attribute (closedby="any") opts a dialog into light-dismiss so clicking the backdrop closes it, aligning dialog with popover behavior in current browsers.

sections.heading: popover: the lightest overlay
sections.body:
The popover attribute turns any element into a hidden overlay that renders in the top layer when shown — the primitive beneath menus, hint bubbles, emoji pickers and toasts. Unlike dialog, a popover is never modal: the page behind stays fully interactive, and by default it light-dismisses — clicking anywhere outside or pressing Escape closes it. That default is popover="auto", which also closes any other open auto-popover, so only one menu is ever open. The variant popover="manual" opts out of light-dismiss for things like persistent toasts that only close explicitly, and popover="hint" (newest) serves hover-style hints that can coexist with an open auto-popover.

The invoker wiring is pure HTML: a button with popovertarget="some-id" toggles the popover with that id. popovertargetaction refines the verb to "show" or "hide" when toggle is wrong — a notification's dismiss button, for instance, is popovertargetaction="hide". The browser maintains the accessibility relationship between invoker and popover, manages the top layer, and fires beforetoggle/toggle events for script that wants to react; showPopover(), hidePopover() and togglePopover() exist for programmatic control.

Styling hooks match dialog's: the open state is selectable with :popover-open, and auto popovers get a ::backdrop pseudo-element (transparent by default, since popovers do not dim the page). Anchoring the popover next to its button is the job of CSS anchor positioning as it matures; until then, popovers center by default like dialogs and are positioned with ordinary CSS.

sections.heading: Choosing the right primitive
sections.body:
Three overlapping tools resolve cleanly once you ask two questions: does the content interrupt, and does it float?

details/summary is for content that neither interrupts nor floats — it expands in place, pushing the page down, and the rest of the page remains fully usable. FAQs, advanced-options sections, long changelogs, collapsible sidebars. If the collapsed content is part of the document's flow, this is the tool, and the name attribute covers the accordion case.

dialog with showModal() is for interruptions: the user must deal with this box before touching anything else. Destructive confirmations, required re-authentication, focused creation flows. Modality is expensive attention-wise, so it should be rare — if you are reaching for a modal to show optional information, you probably want the third tool. popover is for floating, dismissible extras: menus, pickers, hints, toasts — content that overlays without blocking, vanishes on an outside click, and never traps focus. The rough hierarchy of user cost is details (free) < popover (cheap) < modal dialog (expensive); default to the cheapest primitive that satisfies the requirement, and let the browser do the widget engineering it now does better than our libraries did.
